analysis.one_liner: Stops Medicare hospitals from garnishing wages or seizing homes over medical bills, and funds debt buyouts.
analysis.headline: The Patient Debt Relief Act was introduced in July 2024 with 16 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set new rules for hospitals that take Medicare patients. Hospitals would have to publish and apply a charity care policy, screen patients for help before billing, and let patients appeal denials. They could no longer put a lien on a home, garnish wages, or sell most hospital bills to debt collectors, and could not charge interest to families earning under 250% of the poverty line. Hospitals that broke the rules could face fines up to $1 million per violation. A separate program would have given $100 million to a nonprofit to buy up and erase patients' medical debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who owe hospital bills, especially lower-income households. The bill would have forced hospitals to check whether patients qualify for charity care before sending bills, banned the harshest collection tools (home liens, wage garnishment), capped repayment at 4% of gross monthly income before any debt sale, and wiped out debt for people whose bills exceeded 5% of income or who earned under 400% of the poverty line.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals in Medicare would have been required to have a written charity care policy with public minimum eligibility rules and to screen every patient for financial assistance before collecting payment.

Hospitals could no longer place a lien on or foreclose on a patient's home, or garnish wages, to collect a hospital bill; bills could not be sold to a debt collector within a year unless the patient declined or defaulted on a repayment plan capped at 4% of gross monthly income.
Families with household income at or below 250% of the poverty line could not be charged interest on hospital bills, and their debts could not be sold to collectors at all.
Patients would get an appeal if denied charity care, notice of their rights with every bill, a federal portal to report hospital noncompliance, and annual audits of a random sample of hospitals.

A $100 million grant program would fund one nonprofit to identify eligible people and buy up and discharge their medical debt, with notice to each person whose debt is erased and quarterly public reporting.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals would bear the cost of screening patients, processing appeals, and giving up liens, garnishment, interest, and quick debt sales, and could face civil monetary penalties up to $1 million per instance of noncompliance. Debt collectors and debt buyers would lose access to a stream of freshly sold hospital debt. Federal taxpayers would fund the $100 million debt-relief grant.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, debt collectors, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The relief grant is narrow: $100 million for fiscal year 2025 flows to a single nonprofit, so only a fraction of the medical debt carried by American households could be purchased and discharged even in the best case.

Hospitals argue that charity care screening and restrictions on collection increase uncompensated costs and paperwork, which can be absorbed more easily by large systems than by small rural and safety-net hospitals already operating on thin margins.

The bill leaves insurance billing and non-hospital medical debt (physician groups, ambulance services) untouched, so a patient's worst collection exposure could shift to providers the bill does not cover.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing liens, garnishment, and compounding interest on hospital bills, the protections would have been substantial and the compliance burden on hospitals modest compared with hospital revenues. The debt-relief grant was the weakest part: $100 million through one nonprofit cannot match the scale of household medical debt, and one-time buyouts treat symptoms rather than the pricing that creates the debt.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, but neither committee ever held a markup or vote on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Gabe Vasquez introduced the bill on July 24, 2024, with five original cosponsors, and 16 House Democrats cosponsored it in total; no Republican cosponsor joined.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, a dual referral that requires two committees to act.

On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health of Energy and Commerce; no markup, hearing, or floor vote followed, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and medical debt collectors keep their existing collection practices, and patients with hospital debt got no new protections or relief. The bill's cosponsors gained a stated position but no law.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; with Republicans holding the committee chairs and the House majority, the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have barred hospitals from taking patients' homes or wages for hospital debt, capped repayment plans, and imposed fines up to $1 million for noncompliance with charity care screening. Hospitals would have absorbed screening costs and lost the most aggressive collection tools.

Hospitals could no longer sell recent hospital debt, and any collector buying older debt would have had to agree not to garnish wages or foreclose on homes. This would shrink the market for purchased medical debt.

A $100 million grant would fund a nonprofit to buy and discharge patients' medical debt directly. The interest of these organizations runs alongside patients', though the single-grantee structure concentrates the benefit.
